item.title: Getting your app ready for iPhone Duo: what actually broke
item.description: iPhone Duo ships on 23 October, and Duo screenshots become mandatory for new App Store submissions in April 2027. Here is what broke when we ran a real app on it, and the checks I'd do first.
item.content:encoded:
iPhone Duo ships on 23 October, and from April 2027 Apple will ask for Duo screenshots with every new App Store submission. So sooner or later, every iOS app has to look right on it.

We spent the last few weeks running Lake, our coloring and journaling app, on the Duo simulator, screen by screen, with our designers marking every glitch. Lake is mostly UIKit, with the newer screens in SwiftUI.

Lake is iPad-first, so it has always scaled to large screens, and on iPad you can already resize its window to any size you like. Resizability, the thing everyone is so worried about, we thought we had covered. Then Apple announced the Duo and the vertical bar, and that changed the game.

Still, very little of what broke was exotic. Almost all of it came from assumptions that were true on every iPhone until now. Here's the short checklist, then the details, roughly in the order I'd check them.

TL;DR

  1. Three screens, not one. Your app runs in landscape on the inner display even if it only supports portrait, so test it there.
  2. The side safe area. Pin to the safe area horizontally, not to the screen edges.
  3. The vertical bar. Check every screen with a navigation bar, and opt a screen out if its buttons belong at the top.
  4. If you keep the vertical bar. Hiding the status bar doesn't remove the column, so decide with your designers what goes under it.
  5. Breakpoints. Test each one at 466 × 678, 669 × 951 and 951 × 669.
  6. .pad checks. If one really means "big screen", base it on the available space instead of the device.
  7. Folding. Fold and unfold with each screen open, not just at launch.

Three screens, not one

The Duo gives your app three quite different canvases: the cover display when it's folded, and the big inner display, in portrait or landscape.

DisplaySize (pt)Safe area
Cover, folded466 × 67884 pt on the side
Inner, portrait669 × 951at the top, like an iPhone
Inner, landscape951 × 66984 pt on the side

Two things matter more than the numbers.

It's still an iPhone. The inner display reports regular width and height, the same size classes as an iPad. But userInterfaceIdiom is still .phone. Code that checks size classes treats it like an iPad, and code that checks the idiom treats it like an iPhone. Most apps check both, in different places, so you get a mix that nobody designed.

Portrait lock doesn't protect you. The inner display ignores UISupportedInterfaceOrientations. If your iPhone app only supports portrait, it still runs in landscape on the inner display, and every screen that was only ever designed tall and narrow is now wide and short.

The side safe area isn't zero any more

On every iPhone so far, a portrait screen had safeAreaInsets.left and .right at 0. A lot of code quietly relies on that.

On the cover display and in inner landscape, iOS 27 moves the status bar into a vertical bar along one side, the side with the camera. It reserves an 84 pt column for it, and the safe area reports that column as a side inset. Anything pinned to the screen edges ends up underneath it:

The close button on the left is still there. It's hidden under the clock. That was our most common bug: close and share buttons pinned to the top-trailing corner, which on the Duo is exactly where the status bar now lives.

The fix is the boring, well-known one, applied horizontally and not just at the top:

// Before: fine on every iPhone until now
closeButton.trailingAnchor.constraint(
    equalTo: view.trailingAnchor, constant: -20)

// After: follows the vertical bar, whichever side it's on
closeButton.trailingAnchor.constraint(
    equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.trailingAnchor, constant: -20)

In SwiftUI, look for .ignoresSafeArea() on anything that isn't a background.

Other places this showed up for us:

  • Content that looks off-centre. A card centred on the full width sits 42 pt (half the column) off-centre next to content that respects the safe area.
  • Custom popups and sheets. Our own presentation controllers set the horizontal safe area to zero, or pinned the popup to the edges of the screen.

iOS 27's vertical bar

The column isn't just for the status bar. When a screen has a navigation bar, iOS 27 moves its buttons into the same vertical bar:

It's a sensible default, but it breaks layouts that expect their buttons across the top. A view controller can opt out:

override var preferredVerticalBarBehavior: UIVerticalBarBehavior {
    .disabled
}

With the vertical bar disabled, the buttons and the status bar move back to the top, and the side inset goes away: the safe area becomes 82 pt at the top instead of 84 pt on the side. Apple's documentation asks you to use this sparingly, for screens like full-screen players or calculators. It's also not great UX to mix the two too much in one app: if some screens keep their buttons at the top and others move them into the vertical bar, the buttons jump around as people navigate. Apple's documentation makes the same point, asking you to treat the setting as a stable choice. It also warns that a bar button item marked horizontal-only isn't shown at all when there's no horizontal bar, so opt the whole screen out rather than individual buttons.

One more trap, from our own card-style popups: the card itself had no side inset, but the screen inside it still got the window's 84 pt inset from the vertical bar, so its content sat off-centre inside the card. Opting those screens out of the vertical bar fixed it. If you have custom presentations, check the safe area inside them.

If you keep the vertical bar

Turning the vertical bar off is meant for a few special screens, so on most screens the column stays. Two things we expected to help with it didn't.

Hiding the status bar doesn't remove the column. With prefersStatusBarHidden = true, the clock and Wi-Fi icons disappear, but the inset stays at 84 pt and you're left with an empty column. Only turning off the vertical bar gives the space back.

Scroll edge effects don't draw there. Think of a horizontal carousel of cards. It scrolls to the edge of the screen, so its cards slide under the column, behind the clock. Since iOS 26, the obvious fix is a scroll edge effect: the soft fade iOS already draws where content meets the top bar. We tried it on the trailing edge every way we could think of:

  • SwiftUI's scrollEdgeEffectStyle, both .soft and .hard, with and without contentMargins;
  • UIKit's edge effects on a horizontal UIScrollView, both nested inside the page and as the page's own scroll view.

None of them draw anything in the column, while the effect at the top works as usual. A scroll view nested inside another one doesn't even see the side inset: its safe area reports 0.

So treat the column as part of the layout and ask your designers what should be under it. We left it plain on most screens.

Breakpoints that don't expect this shape

Many apps pick a layout from the screen size: a phone layout below some size, a tablet layout above it. Inner landscape is 951 pt wide and only 669 pt tall, a shape no iPhone or iPad has. Ours slipped past the checks for small screens and landed in the iPad layout: iPad spacing on a screen two-thirds the height of an iPad, so some screens ran out of room and their buttons ended up off the bottom.

Search your code for every breakpoint and size-class branch, and check what each one does at 951 × 669 and at 669 × 951. If a rule only looks at width, it's probably wrong for one of them.

Check what you gate on .pad

The opposite problem: features you hid on iPhone because the screen was too small. The Duo is still a .phone, so they stay hidden, even on the big inner display.

Search for userInterfaceIdiom == .pad and decide for each one whether it means "iPad" or "big screen". Ours included an Apple Pencil hover preview. The Duo works with the USB-C Apple Pencil, which supports hover and tilt but not pressure, squeeze or double-tap. So hover was the one premium Pencil feature that would have worked, and we were hiding it.

For anything that's really about room on screen, don't check the idiom at all. Apple has long advised basing layout on the space you actually get (size classes and the size of your view) rather than on the kind of device, and the Duo is exactly why. Keep idiom checks for things that really differ between devices.

Folding happens while your screens are open

On an iPhone, the screen only changes when it rotates, and plenty of apps are locked to portrait, so for them it never changes. On the Duo, folding and unfolding change the size, the size classes, the safe area and the bars, while the user is in the middle of something.

Anything you work out once and keep goes stale: a "current screen size" saved at launch, a status bar setting chosen during a transition, constraints built from safeAreaInsets numbers instead of the layout guide. We found screens that looked right after a fresh launch on the inner display and wrong after unfolding the phone.

UIKit tells you when these change: viewWillTransition(to:with:) for size, viewSafeAreaInsetsDidChange() for the safe area, and trait change registration for size classes. If your layout reads any of these values directly, update it there.

In SwiftUI, most of this happens on its own: views that read horizontalSizeClass from the environment, or simply lay out in the space they're given, update when the phone folds. The stale bugs come from copying those values somewhere, for example measuring a size in onAppear and keeping it in @State. Use onGeometryChange(for:of:action:) instead, which runs again every time the size or the safe area changes.

Test it without a Duo

You don't need hardware for any of this. The iPhone Duo simulator in Xcode 27.1 caught every layout problem above:

  • Device Hub (Xcode 27's replacement for Simulator.app) folds, rotates and taps both displays. Hold Option to get the hinge slider.
  • One screenshot per display: xcrun simctl io <udid> screenshot --display=1 captures the cover and --display=3 the inner display. A plain screenshot always captures the inner display, which is black while the phone is folded.
  • Scripts and AI agents: duoctl folds, rotates and taps the simulator from the command line. All the screenshots in this post were taken with it. My post on scripting the Duo simulator explains how it works.
  • XCUITest runs on the Duo, but it can't fold or rotate it: XCUIDevice.shared.orientation changes nothing there. Put the simulator in the posture you want first, in Device Hub or with duoctl, then run your tests. We've only verified it on the folded phone.

A cheap first pass: open each main screen in all three postures, take a screenshot of each, and put them side by side. Most of the problems above are obvious at a glance.

None of this is hard. It's just a lot of small places where we assumed an iPhone was a fixed, portrait rectangle with the status bar at the top, and the Duo isn't. Start early, and April 2027 will be a non-event.

item.title: Where did my disk go? Xcode, worktrees and AI agents
item.description: Running AI agents on an iOS project in parallel worktrees quietly eats disk space, and when the disk fills up, Xcode reports everything except a full disk. Here's where the space goes, how to measure it honestly and how to keep it under control.
item.content:encoded:
A few weeks ago my builds started failing in strange ways. A linker step died. Then lipo. Then the module cache complained that a file "has been modified since the module file" was built. Clean builds didn't help.

The disk was full. Nothing in those errors said so.

This happens a lot more once AI agents are part of your workflow. I run two or three agents at once, each in its own git worktree, each building the app and running tests. Each worktree also gets its own copies of the simulators. Agents sharing one simulator would install over each other's builds and tap around in each other's screens. Every build, test run and simulator copy leaves gigabytes behind, and none of it cleans up after itself.

TL;DR

  1. When a build fails strangely, run df -h /System/Volumes/Data first.
  2. Trust df, not du: clones make du overstate everything.
  3. Clean up a worktree's DerivedData, test products and simulators when you remove it, with a skill, a hook or both.
  4. Point every build of the same worktree at the same DerivedData.
  5. When space is tight, delete whole regenerable folders, not pieces of them.
  6. Every now and then, open mo analyze and look.

Xcode won't tell you the disk is full

When the disk fills up mid-build, the error you see is rarely "No space left on device". The ones I hit:

  • Linker or lipo failures. These do mention "No space left on device", but buried in a long log.
  • Module cache errors like "has been modified since the module file", left behind by a half-written cache.
  • A wall of build-system errors. One build printed 23 lines of "unexpected incomplete target" and, at the very end, the real cause: database or disk is full.

So the first rule: when a build fails in a way that makes no sense, check the disk before anything else. And read the last error, not the first.

Measure the right thing

Checking free space has two traps of its own.

df -h / lies. On modern macOS, / is the sealed, read-only system volume. One day mine reported 5.2 GB free while the volume where my files actually live was 99% full. Check the data volume instead:

df -h /System/Volumes/Data

du double-counts. Xcode and the simulator copy files with APFS clones, which share their storage until one copy changes. du counts each copy at full size. I once deleted a folder du reported as 3 GB and got about 90 MB back, because DerivedData still held the same blocks. A built worktree of the app I work on looked like twice its real size in du.

So judge any cleanup by how much df changes, not by what du said the folder weighed.

Where the space goes

How much space each of these takes depends on your app: its size, its packages and how many tests you run. What doesn't depend on your app is what grows. All of these live under ~/Library/Developer/:

WhatWhereGrows with
Agent test runsXcodeBuildMCP/workspaces/every test run
Deleted worktreesXcode/DerivedData/every worktree you remove
Cloned simulatorsCoreSimulator/Devices/every clone and its apps
Module cachesXcode/DerivedData/ModuleCache.noindexXcode and SDK updates

For scale, I work on a modular UIKit app of about 300,000 lines of Swift in 70 packages. For me, one test run left 6–7 GB, a built worktree cost 25–30 GB and a cloned simulator about 3 GB. Yours might be a tenth of that, or more.

The first row surprised me most. XcodeBuildMCP, which my agents use to build and test, keeps a full copy of the test products for every test run, outside DerivedData, so Xcode's clean doesn't touch it. One afternoon of UI and snapshot tests left 96 GB there and filled the disk twice.

The second row is the slow leak. Every worktree you delete leaves its DerivedData folder behind, and if you also build it with plain xcodebuild, that's a second folder. I found 65 orphaned folders. You can tell them apart because a live folder has an info.plist whose WorkspacePath points at a project that still exists. An orphan's either has no info.plist or points at a path that's gone.

To see your own numbers, list the biggest folders in each place:

cd ~/Library/Developer
du -sh XcodeBuildMCP/workspaces/* Xcode/DerivedData/* CoreSimulator/Devices/* \
  2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -15

du is fine for finding the big ones. Just don't expect deleting them to free exactly that much (more on that above).

Clean up when the worktree goes

The best moment to clean up is when you remove a worktree. You know exactly what belonged to it, so nothing has to be guessed later:

  1. The worktree and its branch.
  2. Its DerivedData folders: every folder whose info.plist has a WorkspacePath inside the worktree.
  3. Its XcodeBuildMCP workspace, named after the worktree directory (or rather, after where the agent session started; see the update below).
  4. Its simulators. Name your clones after the worktree (I use wt-<ticket>-<device>) and they're easy to find.
  5. Anything else you keep per worktree, like screenshots or test diffs.

I wrote this down as an agent skill: a cleanup-worktree instruction file the agent follows after a PR is merged. It checks that the PR really merged and nothing is left uncommitted, removes everything above and reports how much space came back. It also sweeps orphans from worktrees deleted earlier, but asks before deleting those, because matching them is guesswork.

If you'd rather not depend on remembering to ask, make it automatic. I manage worktrees with worktrunk, which runs hooks when a worktree is removed. A user-level hook could clean the Xcode leftovers every time:

# ~/.config/worktrunk/config.toml
[post-remove]
xcode-leftovers = """
cd ~/Library/Developer
# XcodeBuildMCP names workspaces <worktree>-<12-character hash>
for dir in XcodeBuildMCP/workspaces/*; do
  case "${dir##*/}" in
    {{ worktree_name }}-????????????) rm -rf "$dir" ;;
  esac
done
for plist in Xcode/DerivedData/*/info.plist; do
  case "$(plutil -extract WorkspacePath raw "$plist" 2>/dev/null)" in
    {{ worktree_path }}/*) rm -rf "${plist%/info.plist}" ;;
  esac
done
"""

The skill and the hook complement each other: the hook makes sure the obvious things go every time, and the skill handles the judgement calls, like whether the branch is really merged.

Update, 27 October 2026. One catch I've hit since: XcodeBuildMCP names its workspace after the folder the agent session was started in, not the worktree it's building. Start a session in worktree A, move it on to worktree B, and B's builds and test runs land in A's workspace. Clean up A, and you delete B's test run halfway through. My tests failed with "Cannot launch simulated executable: no file found", and the next run rebuilt everything from scratch.

The fix is a habit rather than a script. Start a new agent session inside each worktree, so each one gets its own workspace on its first build. And before cleaning up a worktree, check that no running session was started there, even if it's busy with something else now. The hook above can't know that, so it's safest for worktrees whose sessions you've already closed.

Stop making new copies

Cleaning up is half of it. The other half is not creating duplicates in the first place.

Share one DerivedData per worktree. My agents build through XcodeBuildMCP, which uses its own DerivedData path. But some scripts called xcodebuild directly, with the default path, so the same worktree got built twice in two places. Now every direct xcodebuild call passes the same -derivedDataPath as the MCP. The second build compiles nothing.

Keep your own Xcode separate. I deliberately left builds from the Xcode app in the default DerivedData. That way, opening a worktree in Xcode never fights an agent's build over the same folder.

Delete whole trees, not pieces. Because of the clones, deleting test products alone frees almost nothing. When the disk is really full, what actually helped was:

  • the module caches (ModuleCache.noindex and SDKExplicitPrecompiledModules), which come back immediately and are rebuilt on the next build;
  • the whole XcodeBuildMCP workspace of a worktree that no longer exists;
  • simulator clones nobody uses.

Look before you clean

Before any of this, it's worth seeing for yourself where the space actually went. Mole (brew install mole) is a free, open-source Mac cleanup tool with a very good disk explorer:

mo analyze

It shows your disk as a tree you can walk through, largest folders first, which is the quickest way to see where the space actually went before you delete anything. It also has mo clean and mo purge for caches and build artifacts, both with --dry-run so you can see what they'd remove first.

I'd run it by hand, though, not give it to an agent. The point is for you to understand where the space goes, and then to automate the parts you understand.

None of this is hard, but none of it happens on its own. Look once with mo analyze to see where your space goes, then let a hook or a skill clean up after every worktree, and you can stop thinking about it.

item.title: Scripting the iPhone Duo simulator: how Device Hub folds, rotates and touches it
item.description: Xcode 27.1 ships an iPhone Duo simulator. Device Hub can fold it, rotate it and tap both of its screens, but nothing scriptable could. So I watched what Device Hub does and built duoctl.
item.content:encoded:
Xcode 27.1 ships an iPhone Duo simulator, and Device Hub (the app that replaced Simulator.app) can fold it, rotate it and tap either of its two screens. By hand. The moment I tried to do any of that from a script, everything fell apart.

More and more of us, iOS developers, let AI agents build our apps, run them on a simulator and check that a layout looks right before a PR goes out. With the Duo, the screen that matters most is the big inner one, and that's exactly the one nothing could reach:

  • Folding. simctl has no hinge or posture command. Neither does devicectl.
  • Rotating. devicectl device orientation set reports success and changes nothing. So does XCUIDevice.shared.orientation in a UI test.
  • Tapping. AXe, XcodeBuildMCP and RocketSim all reported success on the unfolded inner screen. Nothing happened.
  • Screenshots. simctl io screenshot captures the inner screen even when the phone is folded, so you get a black image.

The silent part is what hurts. Every one of those calls exits with 0. An agent happily carries on, takes a screenshot of the wrong screen and tells you the layout looks fine.

Watch what Device Hub does

If Device Hub can do it, the simulator has a way to receive it. So the question was: what does Device Hub send?

The trick is unglamorous. Stream the logs on both sides of the wall: log stream on the Mac for Device Hub and CoreDevice, and xcrun simctl spawn <udid> log stream inside the simulator. Then press the button in Device Hub and read what happens.

Folding: a hidden slider

Folding had already been figured out by Artem Novichkov's hinge. Device Hub has a hidden hinge slider (hold Option), and it sends a vendor-defined HID event (usage page 0xFF61, usage 0x5B) with a small serialized dictionary as its payload:

provider = com.apple.Virtualization
source   = hinge-slider-control
type     = range
value    = 0…180

A tiny helper posts that event from inside the simulator (xcrun simctl spawn), locationd turns it into a hinge angle, and the Duo folds. Device Hub even plays the folding animation.

Rotating: the same event, a different payload

Rotation was where the logs paid off. When I pressed Rotate in Device Hub, the simulator's HID daemon logged "Handling IndigoVendorDefinedEvent" on the same channel as the hinge, about 300 ms before the inner screen changed orientation.

The payload keys were sitting right next to the hinge's, both in Device Hub's iPhone Duo plugin and inside locationd:

provider = com.apple.Virtualization
source   = orientation-picker-control
type     = enum
value    = portrait | pud | landscape-left
           | landscape-right | faceup | facedown

Post that and the Duo rotates. One surprise: the inner screen sits a quarter turn from the cover, so on the inner screen landscape-left is what gives you a portrait interface. Always read the result back instead of trusting the name.

Touches: one touchscreen per screen

Taps were the interesting part. I assumed they were being dropped, the way Xcode 27 drops a tap that arrives too early (AXe #71). They weren't dropped. They were delivered to the wrong screen.

Inside the simulator, every display gets its own touchscreen, each tagged with that display's ID: mainTouchscreen(0x101) for the cover and touchscreen(0x103) for the inner screen. A tap from AXe arrived like this:

Handling IndigoDigitizerEvent
Sending event to service mainTouchscreen(0x101)

That's the cover screen, switched off while the phone is open. When I clicked the inner screen in Device Hub instead, the event went to 0x103.

So the fix had to change where the touch goes, not when. Inside the simulator, I copy the inner screen's touchscreen as a virtual HID device (with the private HID framework's HIDVirtualEventService), keep its display ID, and send finger events through the copy. The first time, Safari's "Not Now" button disappeared on the inner screen. That was a good moment.

It works on the cover too, in every orientation, for taps, long presses and swipes. And because the helper waits until the system confirms the touchscreen is ready, it also sidesteps the Xcode 27 timing bug on ordinary simulators.

I reported the inner-screen routing to AXe as #74, so hopefully the tools we already use can pick it up.

duoctl

I wrapped everything into duoctl, a small command-line tool and agent skill:

duoctl close                   # fold shut
duoctl open --duration 1.5     # unfold, animated
duoctl rotate portrait
duoctl tap --label "Continue"  # inner screen too
duoctl swipe 330 800 330 300
duoctl screenshot shot.png     # whichever screen shows
duoctl state                   # hinge, screen, size

duoctl state and every fold or rotation print JSON with the hinge angle, the active screen, the orientation and the size in points. An agent can check the result instead of hoping.

You can install it as a skill for your agent with skills.sh:

npx skills add skarol/duoctl

or with openskills:

npx openskills install skarol/duoctl

If you'd rather run duoctl yourself, in the terminal or on CI, install it with Homebrew:

brew install skarol/tap/duoctl

It's MIT licensed, and it's Python with a small Objective-C helper, so there's nothing to build.

A fair warning

All of this sits on private, undocumented simulator interfaces, checked with Xcode 27.1 and the iOS 27.1 runtime. A future Xcode may change them. duoctl reads the state back after every fold and rotation, so if that happens you'll get an error, not another silent success.

Have you started testing on the iPhone Duo yet? What's been the hardest part for you? Let me know, and if duoctl breaks on your setup, open an issue.

item.title: Why we fail to keep good-quality software
item.description: When you become a programmer, you hear a lot that you need to deliver good-quality code. The code should be readable and easy to understand for other developers. It should also be maintainable. Oh, and you should write unit tests...
item.content:encoded:
When you become a programmer, you hear a lot that you need to deliver good-quality code. The code should be readable and easy to understand for other developers. It should also be maintainable. Oh, and you should write unit tests. But have you ever seen any project that has a readable code? Is it free of a technical debt? And is easy to maintain? I guess not too often, right?

Have you ever asked yourself why?

Let’s imagine Steve. He is the owner of a small startup and has an excellent (he thinks) idea for a product. He recently got funding for MVP. In 3 months he will need to show something to his investors in order to convince them to continue supporting his idea. He finds a software house that will make his idea a real product.

Now, let’s imagine Bob. He is new to this software house and was recently promoted to mid developer. In his previous jobs, he didn’t have any influence on architecture or technical stack decisions. Finally, he gets to the point when his voice matters. Bob and other developers are asking themselves how they want to help Steve materialize his idea.

He has in his mind everything he has ever heard about good-quality code. He thinks: This time I will make this neatly. This will be a project with thorough architecture, with continuous refactor and high coverage of a unit test. Something to be proud of.

The scope of MVP has been set. The development team has established the architecture and some technical stack. And after two weeks they start to code. The team doesn’t deliver software frequently and Steve is not pleased with the progress. He starts to push developers. Bob and his friends give up on a unit test. But Steve is still fearful. He pushes even more. The team gives up some patterns and then a code review. They stop to pair program and start to do overtime and whatever they need to catch up in time. But Steve keeps pushing.

As you can imagine, this continuous process will eventually lead us to the point where we don’t have any good quality standards. However, Bob and his team have met the deadline. Steve isn’t completely satisfied with the delivered product but at least he has something to show to his investors. Everybody is happy this is finally over.

And now there are two scenarios. In the first one, the product is a piece of crap and investors kill it. In the second one, the investors like it and want to continue funding it. Steve comes back and wants Bob to deliver the next milestone. You can imagine how happy Bob is to work on a legacy code. He swears that this time he will refactor piece by piece. And guess what? The situation repeats itself. This time investors release the product. However, users are disappointed and complain about a number of bugs.

We can ask how this happened, but we’ve all been there. Someone didn’t stop it. Who should have done it?

It could have been anybody who’s aware of a problem, perhaps someone from Development team or even Bob. So why no one tried to fix it? Why don’t you do it when you are a part of that development team?

Most of us, developers, are introverts. We don’t talk too much. Every sentence is carefully considered. It is extremely hard to admit that nothing goes according to the plan. Often you feel pressure, not only from your client but also from people you work with. In this case, you haven’t got any support.

I have no ready solutions or answers. The problem remains and it’s up to us to tackle it or we will keep running around in circles. Why wouldn’t you stop it?
